title: Xi Comes to Washington Armed With a Rare-Earth Card
gist: Ahead of the Trump-Xi Washington summit, China's rare-earth leverage remains largely unanswered: analysts expect a truce extension, but U.S. dependence likely persists into the early-to-mid 2030s and is sharpened by Iran-war munitions depletion.

insights.claim: China retaliated against Trump's April 2025 tariffs with rare-earth export restrictions, leading to a one-year U.S.-China trade truce that expires in November 2026.
insights.speaker: Christina Lu
insights.so_what: Truce expiry in November is a key event risk for trade and minerals markets.

insights.claim: Chinese shipments of rare-earth magnets to the United States dropped again in August, and USTR Jamieson Greer has given China only a 'passing grade' on rare-earth exports.
insights.speaker: Christina Lu
insights.so_what: Ongoing supply fluctuations keep magnet-dependent industries exposed.

insights.claim: The U.S. is unhappy with rare-earth flows but reluctant to do anything that might shut them off, leaving Trump without a real answer to China's leverage.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Welch
insights.so_what: Asymmetric leverage favors China in negotiations; U.S. escalation risk is constrained.
insights.quote: The U.S. is unhappy about the flow of rare earths, but they’re also concerned about doing anything that may shut that off,
insights.locator: “The U.S. is unhappy about the flow

insights.claim: Experts expect both sides to favor a truce extension, with Greer suggesting Washington could support a three-to-six-month extension.
insights.speaker: Christina Lu
insights.so_what: Base case is a short extension, deferring rather than resolving tariff/minerals risk.
insights.quote: Neither side wants to blow this up,

insights.claim: Bloomberg Economics estimates China will dominate rare-earth supply chains from mining through separation and magnet production until at least 2030.
insights.speaker: Christina Lu
insights.so_what: Long runway for Chinese pricing power; non-China producers face long scale-up.

insights.claim: Even if all announced U.S. mineral projects deliver on schedule, Washington's dependence on China will likely persist until the early to mid-2030s.
insights.speaker: Chris Kennedy
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations for near-term payoff from U.S. critical-mineral deals.
insights.quote: Despite all of the investments, all of the deals that the Trump administration has announced since last April, the dependence remains,

insights.claim: Much magnet production outside China, for example in Japan, still relies on Chinese inputs and technology, so dependencies are intermingled at every production stage and must be unwound.
insights.speaker: Chris Kennedy
insights.so_what: 'Friend-shored' supply chains may still carry hidden China exposure.

insights.claim: The Iran war has depleted U.S. critical munitions stockpiles, increasing defense-sector demand for rare earths and exposing reliance on Chinese minerals.
insights.speaker: Chris Kennedy
insights.so_what: Munitions restocking boosts defense demand while raising minerals bottleneck risk.
insights.quote: Given the war in Iran, there’s a greater demand from the U.S. defense sector now to rebuild munitions stockpiles,

insights.claim: Washington has ordered defense contractors to stop sourcing rare earths and certain other minerals from China by Jan. 1, and some contractors are reportedly scrambling to meet the deadline.
insights.speaker: Christina Lu
insights.so_what: Jan. 1 deadline could create cost pressure and supply disruptions for defense primes.
